title: What IMO's MASS Code means for remote control and autonomy at sea
description:
The MASS Code introduces, for the first time, a global regulatory framework for ships operating with remote control and autonomous functions.
In doing so, the MASS Code provides a common framework for evaluating safety and supporting the wider adoption of remote control and autonomous functions.
Why the MASS Code is voluntary One of the most frequently raised questions is why the MASS Code has been adopted as a non-mandatory instrument.
With the MASS Code, the regulatory scope expands to reflect the operational reality of remote control and autonomy.
The road ahead: Building confidence through experience Looking ahead, the most important phase for the MASS Code is not its adoption, but its application.
text:
For years, maritime autonomy has been framed as a question of technology: what can ships do with limited or no human intervention, and how quickly can those capabilities be scaled? With the adoption of IMO’s Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships (MASS) Code, the conversation has shifted.

The MASS Code introduces, for the first time, a global regulatory framework for ships operating with remote control and autonomous functions. Just as importantly, it signals a transition from isolated projects and pilot cases to a more structured approach to designing and operating them.

Risk assessments and flag state involvement remain central to the approval process, but the MASS Code provides a common, structured basis for assessing new operating concepts.

An enabler for wider adoption

The MASS Code has often been described as a regulatory milestone. It is a goal-based and technology-neutral framework that defines outcomes that must be achieved rather than prescribing specific technical solutions. It establishes the principles and requirements that must be satisfied to ensure safe operation.

This distinction is critical. Autonomous operations can take many forms, from decision-support systems on board to fully remote-controlled vessels. The Code reflects this diversity by applying not only to remotely controlled or autonomous ships but also to individual functions. It recognizes that autonomy will be introduced incrementally, function by function and system by system.

In doing so, the MASS Code provides a common framework for evaluating safety and supporting the wider adoption of remote control and autonomous functions.

Why the MASS Code is voluntary

One of the most frequently raised questions is why the MASS Code has been adopted as a non-mandatory instrument. In a regulatory environment often associated with strict compliance, this may appear counterintuitive. In reality, it reflects the diversity of possible applications and the need to let safety frameworks mature through practical experience.

The voluntary approach is therefore strategic: it gives the industry a common set of principles while preserving the flexibility needed to assess different concepts and solutions, and to help innovation scale faster. Central to this approach is the so-called experience-building phase, during which data from projects and operations can be collected, analysed, and shared to further improve the Code.

In practical terms, this means that flag states and their authorized classification societies remain at the centre of approvals. Projects will continue to be assessed case by case, with safety demonstrated through risk assessment, documentation, and validation.

The Code is not a one-size-fits-all answer. It provides structure and a baseline for more standardized, streamlined approvals, while still requiring each concept to be supported by a robust and well-documented approval case. At the same time, it creates the foundation for a future mandatory framework.

From ships to systems – expanding the regulatory perspective

A second important aspect is that the MASS Code brings the wider operating system into scope, beyond the ship itself. Traditionally, maritime regulation, aside from a few exceptions, has centred on the vessel, focusing on its design, equipment, and operation.

With the MASS Code, the regulatory scope expands to reflect the operational reality of remote control and autonomy. The Code recognizes the vessel as part of a wider operating system, where safety depends on the ship, the remote operations centre (ROC), the digital link between them, and the people operating across both ends of that interface.

This is particularly relevant for remote operation concepts involving essential ship functions. The interaction between ship and shore becomes a key safety consideration, and the ROC is recognized as an integral element of the overall system rather than just an operational support function. Safety and security are no longer just questions of onboard capability. Managing risk depends on how multiple components interact in real time.

This means that roles, responsibilities, and interactions between the ship and the ROC must be clearly defined and verified as part of the safety and approval process. As a result, the ROC becomes part of the overall assurance framework and must be documented, verified, and certified.

Core principles for autonomous operations

The MASS Code is built around goals, functional requirements, and expected performance. Together, these provide a common basis for assessing autonomous and remotely controlled functions, with the objective of demonstrating a level of safety equivalent to conventional operations.

First, the Code requires safety to be demonstrated through structured risk assessment. Compliance is demonstrated by showing that the operating concept, functions, and risks have been understood and controlled. Concepts of operation, hazard identification, operational limits, fallback arrangements, and verification evidence therefore become central to the approval case.

Second, human involvement and responsibility remain central. Remote control and autonomy change how responsibility is exercised but do not remove it. The Code requires that a master remains responsible for the ship and capable of intervening when needed, even when not physically on board. The MASS Code therefore provides a framework for defining roles, competence requirements, and intervention capability.

Third, the Code adopts a functional, goal-based approach. It defines what systems must achieve, for example in navigation, connectivity, or emergency response, without dictating how those functions are implemented. This allows the Code to be applied across different technologies and operating concepts, while maintaining a consistent safety benchmark.

Finally, the Code recognizes that learning is part of the process. The experience-building phase provides a framework for collecting and sharing operational experience so that it can inform future development of the Code and support the transition towards a mandatory global instrument.

DNV assurance frameworks and the MASS Code: Distinct roles, complementary value

The MASS Code raises an important question: how can a global regulatory framework be translated into practical assurance for specific ships, functions, and operating concepts? This is where the industry’s existing work on remote control and autonomy becomes particularly relevant.

Over the past decade, DNV has developed frameworks for assessing and assuring remote-control and autonomous operations, covering concept qualification, system qualification, class notations, remote operations, management systems, and operator competence. The objective is to provide a structured and repeatable way to assess new operating concepts while maintaining safety.

These frameworks serve a different purpose from the MASS Code. The Code establishes common expectations for the safe, secure, and environmentally sound operation of ships with remote-control and autonomous functions, defining goals, functional requirements, and expected performance.

DNV’s frameworks operate at a more practical level, translating those expectations into project-specific assurance cases.

The relationship between the MASS Code and these frameworks is therefore complementary. The Code provides the regulatory direction and common language, while assurance frameworks provide the tools for demonstrating how specific concepts meet those expectations. As experience grows through the Code’s experience-building phase, regulatory development and practical implementation will continue to inform one another.

The road ahead: Building confidence through experience

Looking ahead, the most important phase for the MASS Code is not its adoption, but its application. The experience-building phase will play a central role in shaping how the framework evolves, providing the evidence needed to refine requirements and support eventual mandatory adoption. For that reason, industry participation and engagement will be critical to ensuring that practical experience informs future development of the Code.

Important questions remain around the practical allocation of responsibility between the ship, master, and remote operations centre; human oversight and intervention; system performance, connectivity, and fallback arrangements; data access and use of operational experience; and specific areas such as search and rescue, cybersecurity, and cross-border operation. Addressing these issues will require continued collaboration between industry, regulators, and class. Through independent assurance, technical expertise, and structured verification, class can help turn experience from projects and operations into clearer expectations for the future development of the MASS Code.

name: International Maritime Organization
title: Qatar Participates in 12th Session of the Sub-Committee on the Implementation of IMO Instruments
description:
Doha, July 27 (QNA) – The State of Qatar, represented by its Permanent Delegation to the International Maritime Organization (IMO), has participated in the twelfth session of the Sub-Committee on the Implementation of IMO Instruments, which was recently held at the IMO headquarters in London, UK.
This participation reflects Qatar’s commitment to supporting international efforts aimed at developing mechanisms for implementing international maritime instruments and conventions, ensuring their effective implementation, and enhancing member states’ compliance with international requirements related to maritime safety and security and the protection of the marine environment.
This contributes to raising safety and efficiency levels in the maritime transport sector and protecting lives, property, and the marine environment.
During its meetings, the Committee discussed several technical and organizational topics related to the implementation of IMO instruments, including monitoring the Member States Audit Scheme, analyzing maritime accidents and drawing lessons learned, reviewing data and procedures related to port state control, and enhancing the performance of flag, port, and coastal states in fulfilling their international obligations.

title: Study warns EU ETS carbon cost recovery right may fail in practice - SAFETY4SEA
description:
As explained in the paper “EU ETS payments in shipping: parties’ responsibilities towards authorities and within the commercial chain,” the current EU ETS statutory reimbursement mechanism is structurally flawed.
If the statutory reimbursement right cannot be relied upon, parties throughout the shipping chain need to make sure their own contracts are watertight on carbon cost allocation.
The researchers found that, in practice, responsibility for carbon costs is determined by commercial contracts such as charterparties and management agreements rather than by the statutory mechanism.
As a result, the researchers argue that the reimbursement mechanism has limited practical value for much of the industry.
The EU ETS gives the impression that shipowners and managers who pay the carbon bill can automatically recover it from the party actually responsible for the ship’s operation or fuel purchase.
text:
As explained in the paper “EU ETS payments in shipping: parties’ responsibilities towards authorities and within the commercial chain,” the current EU ETS statutory reimbursement mechanism is structurally flawed. Because it does not adequately account for private international law or the commercial realities of shipping, the researchers argue that the national reimbursement obligation is largely a “paper tiger.”

According to the study, the EU ETS Directive creates the impression that a statutory reimbursement obligation is sufficient and that contractual arrangements are unnecessary. In practice, however, clearly defined contractual responsibilities for purchasing and surrendering EU Allowances (EUAs) are essential. Without them, and without owners having access to voyage and fuel consumption data, carbon cost exposure remains a significant risk.

If the statutory reimbursement right cannot be relied upon, parties throughout the shipping chain need to make sure their own contracts are watertight on carbon cost allocation. Expecting that the statutory mechanism will be sufficient is a risky strategy

… commented Jolien Kruit, co-author of the study, endowed professor “Future of Maritime Law” at Erasmus School of Law and partner at Van Traa Advocaten.

The researchers found that, in practice, responsibility for carbon costs is determined by commercial contracts such as charterparties and management agreements rather than by the statutory mechanism. The study identifies three key obstacles to enforcing the reimbursement right:

Uncertainty over which party is liable in complex charter chains.

Conflicts with English law, which governs most shipping contracts.

The prevalence of arbitration outside the EU, where the statutory right may not be recognized.

As a result, the researchers argue that the reimbursement mechanism has limited practical value for much of the industry.

The research also finds that standard BIMCO clauses provide a useful framework for allocating ETS costs but are not sufficient on their own. They must be incorporated consistently throughout the contractual chain and may require additional provisions covering issues such as price volatility, off-hire, demurrage, and dispute resolution.

The EU ETS gives the impression that shipowners and managers who pay the carbon bill can automatically recover it from the party actually responsible for the ship’s operation or fuel purchase. Our research shows that this is largely an illusion once you look at how shipping contracts actually work

… said Hannah Mosmans, co-author and PhD researcher at the Department of Law and Markets, Erasmus School of Law, and Erasmus UPT, Erasmus University Rotterdam.

The findings have implications beyond the EU. The researchers note that the UK’s domestic shipping emissions trading scheme, which began on July 1, 2026, contains no statutory reimbursement right, while the IMO’s proposed Net Zero Framework could face similar challenges if it does not account for the realities of shipping contracts and private international law.

The authors conclude that future carbon pricing mechanisms should be designed with these commercial and legal complexities in mind.

text:
The sole focus of the 2026 Propulsion & Future Fuels Conference’s opening Keynote Panel discussion – potential IMO global shipping emission changes confirmed at MEPC 85 – will benefit from the valued additional expertise of Dipl.-Ing Torsten Mundt.

A senior policy officer at the German Federal Ministry of Transport, Mundt is responsible for technical issues under MARPOL Annex VI of the International Maritime Organization (IMO), focusing on greenhouse gas and air pollutant reduction in maritime transport.

He is also involved with the Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC) and other EU bodies, and is the head of Germany’s delegation to the IMO Sub-Committee on Pollution Prevention and Response (PPR).

As previously announced, this year’s Propulsion & Future Fuels Conference in Hamburg was postponed to 8-10 December to follow on from the meeting of the IMO’s Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC) from 30 November to 3 December, with the committee’s Second Extraordinary Session scheduled for 4 December.

Whatever emerges from the MEPC meeting will be of significant interest to the global maritime leaders gathered in Hamburg, and could include adoption of a new Emission Control Area (ECA) in the North-East Atlantic with stricter vessel emission limits on Nox, Sox and particulate matter (PM) taking effect in 2028.

Joining Torsten Mundt in assessing the possible effects of MEPC regulations will be conference Chairman Lars Robert Pedersen, the Deputy Secretary General of BIMCO who will first deliver a Keynote Address – IMO Development Update & Mid Term Measures – before joining the panel discussion.

This will be moderated by Markus Munz, Managing Director of VDMA Large Engines, and will also include Wolfram Gunterman, Director of Regulatory Affairs at Hapag-Lloyd AG, alongside other speakers who will be announced in due course.

title: Bangladesh shipbreakers push back against stricter environmental standards
description: DHAKA — Ships sail oceans all over the world, yet as they reach the end of their lives, they mostly go to die on the beaches of Bangladesh, India and Pakistan. text:
DHAKA — Ships sail oceans all over the world, yet as they reach the end of their lives, they mostly go to die on the beaches of Bangladesh, India and Pakistan.

Around 85% of the world’s end-of-life ships are dismantled and recycled in these three South Asian countries, an industry that has long relied on low-cost manual labor but has also been criticized for its high disregard for worker safety and severe environmental pollution.

Shipbreaking is so hazardous that the industry was shut down in industrialized countries in the 1960s, displaced to less-industrialized countries, particularly in South Asia.

Data from the NGO Shipbreaking Platform, which campaigns for improved ship-recycling standards, show that since 2009, 8,221 ships have ended up on South Asian beaches, 480 workers have died on the job, and 520 have been injured. The numbers don’t account for pollution so severe that fish stocks have declined in these areas, putting local fishers out of work.

The future of Bangladesh’s ship recycling industry now hinges on a dispute over two international treaties: the Basel Convention, which regulates the transboundary movement of hazardous waste, and the Hong Kong International Convention for the Safe and Environmentally Sound Recycling of Ships (HKC), a sector-specific treaty adopted under the International Maritime Organization (IMO).

Bangladesh ratified both conventions: Basel in 1993, and HKC in 2023. The latter came into force in 2025, while the former entered into force in 1992.

Government position sparks industry concern

In November 2025, Bangladesh’s interim government reportedly submitted a policy position to the Basel Convention Secretariat, arguing that the Hong Kong Convention cannot replace the Basel Convention procedures governing the transboundary movement of end-of-life ships. The submission proposed that both conventions should continue to apply simultaneously to the shipbreaking industry.

This upset Bangladeshi shipbreakers, who said the move could make ship recycling more costly and complicated, and that it might lead to the closure of the industry in the country. The Bangladesh Ship Breakers and Recyclers Association (BSBRA) has urged the new government, which took office in February, to withdraw that position.

In 2004, it was the countries that had signed up to Basel who invited the IMO to develop mandatory international rules specifically for ship recycling, eventually leading to the adoption of the Hong Kong Convention in 2009. However, they never agreed that the HKC provides an equivalent level of environmental protection.

Beaching remains the biggest divide

The most contentious difference between the two conventions concerns “beaching,” the method in which ships are deliberately grounded on tidal beaches before being dismantled.

Basel’s “Technical Guidelines for the Environmentally Sound Management of the Full and Partial Dismantling of Ships” require dismantling activities to take place on impermeable surfaces capable of containing hazardous materials, effectively ruling out traditional beaching. The HKC, however, permits beaching, provided that shipbreaking yards meet specified safety and environmental standards.

For Bangladeshi recyclers, this distinction is crucial.

Mohammad Mohsin Chowdhury, president of the BSBRA, told Mongabay that the Hong Kong Convention is better suited to South Asia’s economic realities, calling it “customized for the subcontinent’s reality: its [work] culture, community and environment.”

“Following any convention is difficult for us given the human resources we have; we still want our future generation to have a safe environment, and we are working on bringing shipbreaking under regulation,” he added.

“Since we are following HKC regulations, improving the industry and enjoying the benefits, we don’t see why include Basel into shipbreaking affair. It will be an extended burden for shipbreakers.”

Asked whether Basel’s opposition to beaching is why shipbreakers oppose it, Chowdhury said: “This is one of the main reasons, but I think Basel is not concerned about protecting our industry. Following Basel regulations may lead to the closure of the shipbreaking industry.”

“HKC is more suitable for us,” he reiterated. “Basel thinks about the environment, but nothing can be changed overnight.”

Commercial shipbreaking in Bangladesh began in the early 1970s, and the sector boomed in the 1980s, turning the country into a major global hub for ship recycling. But dire working conditions, high rates of fatalities, exploitation of underaged workers, and severe pollution of the marine environment by hazardous waste continued unabated for around five decades. The industry only started to pay heed when many industrialized countries began to ban the beaching method for the dismantling of ships registered in their jurisdictions, and started pushing for a safer environment for workers.

Europe’s standards remain out of reach

The EU Ship Recycling Regulation, adopted in 2013, strictly prohibits the beaching method used in South Asia, and requires all European-flagged vessels to be dismantled at certified “green” yards, predominantly located in Europe, Turkey, and North America. European ship owners account for around 30% of the world’s fleet in tonnage.

According to the BSBRA, 23 shipbreaking yards in Bangladesh’s Chattogram region received green certification under the Hong Kong Convention. However, none of them are listed on the official EU list of approved ship-recycling facilities.

“This is definitely a great loss for us, but ship dismantling on dry docks is very expensive,” Chowdhury said. “We’ll need to spend a whole year’s budget to build just one dry dock.

“I think Basel Convention is partial [to developed countries], maybe it wants to protect their interests,” he added. “Perhaps they want ships to be recycled in an expensive way, and we end up buying more expensive products made with the salvaged metal.”

Environmentalists call for stricter standards

Environmental activists have rejected the industry’s argument.

Syeda Rizwana Hasan, chief executive of the Bangladesh Environmental Lawyers Association (BELA), led the country’s environment ministry in 2025 as an adviser to the interim government at the time. She questioned why the ministry should permit shipbreaking on beaches if the Basel Convention prohibits it.

She also said the Hong Kong Convention primarily reflects the interests of the shipping industry, given that it’s administered by the IMO.

“HKC is monitored by IMO. IMO is a clubhouse of shipowners. It is protecting their interests,” Rizwana Hasan said.

“Nobody wants their waste-laden ships nowadays. Pakistan used to scrap them, now they don’t do that much; shipbreakers in Kolkata, Madras in India don’t take them … only Gujarat and Bangladesh do,” she said. “South Korea stopped it, while China has banned beaching through legal processes.”

She also accused local shipbreakers of not wanting to be regulated — “That’s why they don’t want to comply with Basel Convention” — and alleged that Bangladesh continues to import hazardous ships through inaccurate declarations — something that Basel is specifically designed to prevent.

Rejecting claims that stronger environmental rules would destroy the industry, Rizwana Hasan cited the example of Bangladesh’s garment sector after the 2013 Rana Plaza factory collapse, which killed more than 1,100 people and prompted sweeping reforms to improve workplace safety.

“Everyone thought the garment industry would collapse,” she said. “Instead, compliance improved and the industry became stronger.”

Noting that Bangladesh had ratified the Basel Convention decades ago, Rizwana Hasan said that “no new position has been taken; what we did is a reiteration of what is existing.”

Many environmental organizations argue that the Hong Kong Convention still falls short of guaranteeing environmentally sound ship recycling. Ingvild Jenssen, founder and executive director of the NGO Shipbreaking Platform, said the convention requires significant strengthening.

“Clearly, the Hong Kong Convention does not set a standard that ensures safe and environmentally sound practices,” she said in a statement on the organization’s website. “Now under review at the IMO, it will be key to bolster its requirements, including ways to phase out the fatally flawed beaching method. At the same time, better enforcement of the Basel Convention’s restrictions on hazardous waste trade needs to be ensured through measures that effectively hold the shipping industry accountable. This entails shifting responsibility to the states that actually have control over the owners of assets intended for disposal.”

title: Chain of custody models discussed at IMO expert workshop
description:
The IMO LCA framework, which refers to the IMO framework on life cycle greenhouse gas intensity of marine fuels, includes the development of guidelines on requirements and procedures for recognition of Sustainable Fuel Certification Schemes (SFCS Guidelines) to ensure traceability of fuel sustainability characteristics across the entire fuel supply chain.
At the request of MEPC 84, the Secretariat organized an Expert Workshop (15 July) on chain of custody models for fuel supply traceability with the aim of enhancing the understanding of these models (such as physical segregation, mass balance or book and claim) and how these could be integrated into the IMO LCA framework.
The LCA framework is a key component of future IMO GHG reduction measures.
The workshop provided an opportunity to better understand experiences from chain of custody models in other sectors, which IMO could benefit from in its further work, notably in the context of sustainable marine fuel certification.
Information and views expressed in the workshop are expected to help further develop the LCA Guidelines and draft SFCS Guidelines.
text:
The IMO LCA framework, which refers to the IMO framework on life cycle greenhouse gas intensity of marine fuels, includes the development of guidelines on requirements and procedures for recognition of Sustainable Fuel Certification Schemes (SFCS Guidelines) to ensure traceability of fuel sustainability characteristics across the entire fuel supply chain. One of the core principles of the draft guidelines is to implement a rigorous and structured system for assessing fuels’ well-to-tank (WtT) GHG emissions, incorporating traceability and chain of custody mechanisms to ensure transparency and avoid double counting.

At the request of MEPC 84, the Secretariat organized an Expert Workshop (15 July) on chain of custody models for fuel supply traceability with the aim of enhancing the understanding of these models (such as physical segregation, mass balance or book and claim) and how these could be integrated into the IMO LCA framework. The LCA framework is a key component of future IMO GHG reduction measures.

The workshop provided an opportunity to better understand experiences from chain of custody models in other sectors, which IMO could benefit from in its further work, notably in the context of sustainable marine fuel certification. Experts emphasized the vast experience already gained in using mass balance and the importance of alignment among frameworks. Information and views expressed in the workshop are expected to help further develop the LCA Guidelines and draft SFCS Guidelines.

text:
The Sub-Committee on Implementation of IMO Instruments (III) brings together flag, port and coastal States to consider implementation issues, including the analysis of consolidated audit summary reports from the mandatory IMO Member state Audit Scheme. Following the conclusion on the Sub-Committee, Lloyd’s Register (LR) has provided the following overview of some of the significant outcomes from III 12:

1. Draft amendments to the “Procedures for Port State Control, 2025”

The Procedures for Port State Control, 2025 A.1206(34), while not mandatory, are widely implemented and referenced by regional Port State Control (PSC) regimes (e.g. Paris MoU, Tokyo MoU) and are regarded as the global benchmark for PSC inspections. The Procedures are typically revised every two years to reflect amendments to IMO instruments and evolving inspection practices.

The following proposals for the 2027 revision of the PSC Procedures were considered and progressed as follows:

A new appendix providing harmonized guidance for Port State Control Officers (PSCOs) on the inspection of ship machinery and maintenance systems.

It is recognized that machinery-space inspections and the assessment of maintenance arrangements can be technically challenging, and that the current PSC Procedures lack detailed guidance in this area. Dedicated guidance to support more consistent and effective inspections has been developed.

Amendments to section 1.9 of the PSC Procedures concerning PSCO qualifications.

It was discussed that requiring a PSCO to be qualified as a flag State surveyor may unnecessarily be restrictive. However, it was emphasized that the issue was not whether PSCOs should be competent, as the need for competent PSCOs worldwide was undisputed, but rather the appropriate minimum entry requirements and training pathways for officers entering the PSC system.

Draft appendix 21 covering list of instruments relevant to PSC Procedures.

The list includes but is not limited to MEPC.400(83) Amendments to the 2021 Guidelines on the operational carbon intensity reduction factors relative to reference lines (CII reduction factors guidelines, G3), A.1204(34) Code on Alerts and Indicators, 2025 etc.

However, due to time constraints, the work could not be completed during the session and will continue intersessionally, with finalization currently expected at III 13 (July 2027). Once finalized the revised PSC Procedures are expected to be implemented from 1 January 2028.

2. Survey Guidelines under the Harmonized System of Survey and Certification (HSSC)

a. Draft amendments to 2025 HSSC Survey Guidelines (A.1207(34))

The Survey Guidelines under the Harmonized System of Survey and Certification (HSSC) are regularly reviewed and updated to accommodate new regulatory requirements. While these guidelines are not made mandatory by the IMO, the guidelines are mandatory for all European Union Recognized Organizations (most IACS members) under EU Regulation 391/2009.

The development of the 2027 edition of the HSSC Survey Guidelines has been initiated with work expected on:

Draft amendments arising from mandatory instruments that have entered into force, or are expected to enter into force, by 31 December 2027, including the Hong Kong Convention, together with any amendments adopted under the SOLAS four-year cycle with entry into force dates between 2028 and 2029;

Draft amendments related to the new SOLAS regulation V/23 on Pilot Transfer Arrangements and the associated Performance Standards; and

A Draft Coding System for Remote Surveys, to be incorporated into the HSSC Guidelines to indicate the remote survey eligibility of individual survey items.

The revision of the Survey Guidelines will continue intersessionally, and is expected to be finalized at III 13, and adopted at Assembly 35 (December 2027), with an anticipated implementation date of 1 January 2028.

b. Method for developing and assigning a coding system to update the Survey Guidelines under the HSSC

As part of its work on enabling remote surveys under the HSSC Survey Guidelines, there was broad agreement on the overall framework for identifying whether HSSC survey items are eligible for remote surveys, including:

Adding a new “Remote survey eligible” column to the Survey Guidelines under the HSSC.

Using a three-code system:

Y = Eligible for remote survey.

N = Not eligible.

C = Conditionally eligible, subject to specified criteria.

Converting the existing Guidelines into a tabular format with standard headings:

Code

Survey Item

Survey Requirements

Eligibility for Remote Survey (Y/C/N)

Applying the coding based on normal operating circumstances, while recognizing that Administrations may authorize remote surveys on a case-by-case basis in exceptional situations.

However, due to the complexity of the task and time constraints, the coding system was not finalized. The work is expected to continue intersessionally, with finalization expected at III 13 (July 2027).

3. Amendments to MSC/Circ.1140 – MEPC/Circ.424 on Transfer of ships between States

Concerns were raised about ships that are deregistered by a flag state for non-compliance with statutory requirements before securing registration with a new flag State. To address this gap, draft amendments to MSC/Circ.1140 – MEPC/Circ.424 were developed which introduce a notification mechanism under which flag States would inform the IMO when a ship is deregistered without a new registration. The objective is to improve information sharing through the IMO and enhance Member States’ awareness of ships that may temporarily operate without a flag.

The draft amendments will be submitted to MSC 112 and MEPC 85 for approval (November–December 2026), where they may also consider whether related legal issues should be referred to the IMO Legal Committee.

Further, the potential safety, environmental protection and seafarer welfare risks associated with stateless or abandoned ships were noted, as well as broader legal issues concerning the responsibilities of former flag States and the jurisdiction of port States. This was referred to the Legal Committee for further consideration.

Additional outcomes

As presented by LR, other significant advancements made during the session include:

1. Marine Casualty Investigation

Several documents were considered including the report of the intersessional correspondence group on the Analysis of Marine Safety Investigation Reports. Consequently the sub-committee:

approved a III.3 circular with 70 case studies and lessons learned from marine casualties. Each case study provides an outline of what and why the casualty happened, and identifies key safety issues. Practical lessons learnt aimed at ship operators, managers, owners, officers, and crew are provided;

approved the draft III.3 circular on the Analysis of incidents involving ruptured high-pressure cylinders for dissemination to the maritime industry. The analysis found corrosion as the primary cause of cylinder failures, followed by overpressure and other contributing factors such as recurring deficiencies in inspections, record-keeping, and the management of ageing or overdue cylinders.

agreed to the draft new output proposal for fire standards for cargo handling spaces of specialized self-unloading bulk carriers, which will be submitted to MSC 112 (December 2026) for consideration. Previously it had been acknowledged that cargo handling spaces on self-unloading bulk carriers pose a high fire risk, primarily due to inadequate fire safety standards and regulations, especially around fire detection/extinguishing systems near conveyor belts; and

agreed to the draft new output proposal amending the LSA Code for addressing risks involved with wearing inflatable lifejackets, with a view to consideration by MSC 112 (December 2026). Previously the safety concerns associated with wearing inflatable lifejackets had been acknowledged, particularly the risks of entrapment in water underneath the upturned hull and the need for users to know how to safely deflate and remove the lifejacket in emergency situations.

Additionally, the Bulk Carrier Casualty Report for 2016-2025 was considered, noting that cargo liquefaction remains the greatest contributor to loss of life, while grounding remains the greatest cause of ship losses.

2. Review of the Casualty Investigation Code and the associated implementation Guidelines

The IMO has initiated a review of the Code of the International Standards and Recommended Practices for a Safety Investigation into a Marine Casualty or Marine Incident (MSC.255(84)) and the associated Guidelines to assist investigators in the implementation of the Casualty Investigation Code (A.1075(28)), with a target completion year of 2028. The review was driven by concerns regarding the quality, consistency and timeliness of marine casualty investigations and reports.

To address the issues, the draft amendments to MSC.255(84) and A.1075(28) have been developed. However, due to time constraints, the work could not be completed during the session and will continue intersessionally, with finalisation currently expected at III 13 (July 2027).

3. Review of the list of certificates and documents required to be carried on board ships

As part of the periodic review and update of the IMO circular FAL.2/Circ.133–MEPC.1/Circ.902–MSC.1/Circ.1646–LEG.2/Circ.4, List of Certificates and Documents Required to be Carried on Board Ships, 2022, a revised list was agreed to reflect recent regulatory developments and new certification requirements. It was agreed to include the Guidelines on carriage and use of electronic nautical publications (ENP) system (MSC.1/Circ.1705) under the nautical charts and publications, and the MASS Safety Certificate under other certificates and documents which are not mandatory, based on resolution MSC.595(111).

The revised circular is expected to be submitted to MEPC 85, MSC 112, LEG 114 and FAL 51 for approval (expected by August 2027).

4. Comprehensive revision of the Guidelines on the implementation of the ISM Code by Administrations and companies

Following a study which concluded that the ISM Code itself remains broadly fit for purpose, but that its implementation could be improved, the IMO had previously agreed to undertake a comprehensive revision of the ISM implementation guidelines (resolution A.1188(33) for Administrations and MSC-MEPC.7/Circ.8 for Companies).

Proposals were considered to modernize the implementation guidelines, focusing on digitalization, remote audits, oversight arrangements, and evolving company structures, with the aim of ensuring effective and consistent safety management across the shipping industry.

However, due to time constraints, the work could not be completed during the session and will continue intersessionally, with finalization currently expected at III 13 (July 2027).

text:
EWABA has welcomed the European Commission’s proposed revision of the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS), describing it as a meaningful step towards meeting the bloc’s 2040 climate target while bolstering industrial competitiveness and energy security.

EWABA said the draft text rightly strengthens support for renewable fuels in hard‑to‑abate transport segments, particularly maritime and aviation.

The association highlighted the creation of the Sustainable Maritime Alternative Propulsion (SMAP) mechanism as a major advance, offering long‑term investment certainty for renewable fuel producers and sending a clear signal to investors and suppliers. EWABA also praised provisions recognising the value of European renewable fuel production, noting that domestic output enhances resilience and reduces reliance on imported fossil fuels.

However, EWABA warned that two targeted adjustments are essential for the proposal to deliver its full potential.

First, the association called for explicit inclusion of Annex IX Part B biofuels – notably used cooking oil (UCO) and animal‑fat biodiesel – within the SMAP mechanism.

As drafted, SMAP applies only to Annex IX Part A feedstocks, excluding the most widely available and commercially deployed renewable fuels currently used in maritime transport. EWABA said Part B biodiesel already enables immediate emissions reductions without engine modifications or new bunkering infrastructure and excluding it would undermine the proposal’s decarbonisation goals.

Second, EWABA urged policymakers to ensure sustainability remains the core criterion for feedstock sourcing.

The group cautioned against linking support to geographical origin, arguing that Europe lacks sufficient domestic waste and residue feedstocks to meet demand. Imports of sustainable Annex IX materials are therefore indispensable. EWABA said EU rules should reward verified sustainability and full traceability, supported by the expanding Union Database, rather than location‑based preferences.

EWABA concluded that, with these adjustments, the EU ETS revision would deliver a more effective, technology‑neutral framework capable of accelerating emissions reductions while strengthening Europe’s renewable fuels industry.

text:
Prodevelop S.L., in consortium with CENIT and local partner WKN Trading Enterprise CC, will support the technical implementation of a digital port call optimisation platform at two ports in Namibia. The project will demonstrate how real-time data sharing across port community stakeholders can reduce vessel waiting times, improve operational efficiency, and support measurable reductions in greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from ships while in port.

The 18-month implementation period for the pilot project, under the Global MTCC Network (GMN) Phase II project implemented by the International Maritime Organization (IMO) and funded by the European Union (EU), builds on the pilot announced by the IMO in November 2025 and marks the transition from technology identification to full implementation on the ground. The platform will be deployed at the Ports of Walvis Bay and Lüderitz, where the pilot is anticipated to support up to 7% GHG emission reductions annually for ships while in port. Continuous data collection throughout the pilot will help assess environmental benefits and support consideration of wider adoption across African ports.

The implementation will be carried out by a consortium led by Prodevelop S.L., a Spanish technology company specialised in port logistics and maritime digitalisation, working alongside CENIT, an innovation unit of CIMNE, a Barcelona-based research centre with a strong track record in EU-funded maritime decarbonisation projects. WKN Trading Enterprise CC will provide essential local support, on-site coordination, and knowledge transfer to Namibian port personnel throughout the project.

The Namibian Ports Authority (NAMPORT), as the primary beneficiary, will participate in the deployment and use the platform at both ports. The pilot will be implemented in close coordination with MTCC Africa, the Maritime Technology Cooperation Centre established under GMN Phase I to promote sustainable maritime practices and energy- efficient technologies across the African region.

At the heart of the technical solution is POSIDONIA OPERATIONS – Port Call Optimization), a SaaS based digital platform developed by Prodevelop. The platform enables real-time data sharing among port community stakeholders, including port authorities, terminal operators, shipping agents, pilots, and tugboat companies. This supports better sequencing and management of every vessel call.

The platform implements standardised APIs aligned with the DCSA Just-In-Time (JIT) Port Call Programme and the International Taskforce on Port Call Optimisation (ITPCO). This supports interoperability and replicability across port contexts.

The GHG emission calculation methodology is rooted in the EMEP-EEA guidelines and builds on experience from the European PIONEERS project, with relevant applications in ports including Barcelona (Spain) and the Port of Antwerp and Bruges (Belgium).

The implementation will pursue four core objectives.

1. Improve operational performance by enabling real-time data sharing that can reduce vessel waiting times, optimise berth planning, and support more efficient port call processes, helping to reduce unnecessary fuel use while ships are in port.

2. Support the measurement and reduction of GHG emissions, with individual pollutant and emission figures (CO2, NOx, SOx) quantified per vessel call, aggregated monthly, and benchmarked against a pre-project baseline to demonstrate measurable environmental progress.

title: The Week in Alt Fuels: EU omits e-fuel earmarking – ENGINE - Cyprus Shipping News
description:
The European Commission has proposed amendments and additions to the current EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) as part of its revision, published on 17 July.
The most commonly discussed RFNBO bunker fuels are e-ammonia, e-methanol and e-methane, which are all green hydrogen derivatives.
Zero-emission propulsion technologies would be covered at 90% of the additional deployment and operating cost, scaled to the emissions cuts achieved.
But there are still some unanswered questions around how prices of low- and zero-emission fuels would be determined.
Low- and zero-emission fuels produced from feedstocks sourced in the EU would receive an additional 10 percentage points of fuel price cap coverage.
text:
The EU’s revised ETS could reserve 110 million allowances to reduce green bunker fuel price premiums from 2028-2040. But the absence of dedicated e-fuel earmarking raises some concerns.

The European Commission has proposed amendments and additions to the current EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) as part of its revision, published on 17 July. One of the additions includes a new Sustainable Maritime Alternative Propulsion (SMAP) mechanism to help fund shipping’s transition away from fossil bunker fuels.

Under the new Article 3gaa of the ETS Directive, the Commission would reserve a maximum of 110 million EU Allowances (EUAs) between 1 January 2028 and 31 December 2040 for shipping companies using fuels or propulsion technologies with low- and zero-emission potential, including electric and wind-assisted systems.

The EUAs are intended to cover part of the price differential between conventional fossil bunker fuels and eligible alternatives, as well as the additional costs of deploying zero-emission propulsion systems on ships.

Coverage rates are tiered by fuel type.

For instance, a shipowner that bunkers renewable fuels of non-biological origin (RFNBOs) would receive EUAs worth 90% of the price difference between the fuel and conventional bunker fuel. The most commonly discussed RFNBO bunker fuels are e-ammonia, e-methanol and e-methane, which are all green hydrogen derivatives.

Zero-emission propulsion technologies would be covered at 90% of the additional deployment and operating cost, scaled to the emissions cuts achieved.

Low-carbon hydrogen and its derivatives would be covered at 80%, while biogas and advanced biofuels would be covered at 55% of the price gap. In practice that mostly means blue hydrogen, produced from fossil fuel with carbon capture.

But there are still some unanswered questions around how prices of low- and zero-emission fuels would be determined. It is unclear whether calculations would include energy adjustments to account for differences in energy density between fuel types, and whether it would net out existing EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime cost reductions, including FuelEU’s pooling mechanism.

The Commission has also not clarified where it would source its “average market prices” from, how frequently those prices would be updated or how the scheme would handle cases where a shipping company’s actual bunker price differs from the published reference price.

The proposal also includes bonus percentage points in certain cases.

Low- and zero-emission fuels produced from feedstocks sourced in the EU would receive an additional 10 percentage points of fuel price cap coverage. So would fuels produced in countries with emissions trading systems linked to the EU ETS such as the Swiss ETS, and countries participating in the EU’s proposed “ETS as a service” mechanism.

“ETS as a service” was proposed in Article 25b of the revision and could let the EU help non-EU countries price 50% of shipping emissions on EU-to-non-EU voyages that currently fall outside the EU ETS’s scope. The resulting allowance revenue from that 50% would go to the non-EU country that opts for the service, rather than to the EU as with the ETS.

Fuels used on voyages between EU ports and island ports under a member state’s jurisdiction would receive a further five percentage points across all fuel categories. This could for example be a voyage between Rotterdam-Palermo, which is on the island of Sicily and part of the Italian jurisdiction.

Propulsion technologies installed in EU shipyards would also qualify for an additional five percentage points.

Liner shipping trade body World Shipping Council (WSC) welcomed the mechanism, saying it follows the same policy approach already used in aviation.

“Helping close the price gap between conventional and alternative fuels can encourage uptake, support investment in production and position Europe as a leading alternative fuel bunkering hub,” WSC said.

“Under the plan, up to 100% of the price premium for renewable fuels of non-biological origin used in shipping could be subsidised. That could be significant for fuels such as green ammonia, e-methanol and other hydrogen-based maritime fuels, where cost remains one of the main barriers to early deployment,” the International Association for Hydrogen Safety (HySafe) said in a LinkedIn post.

While the percentages determine how much of the renewable-fossil fuel price gap can be covered for each fuel, they do not guarantee the funding needed to deliver the fuels.

The mechanism would allow all eligible fuels and technologies to draw from a single pool of 110 million EUAs rather than ring-fencing allowances by fuel type. RFNBOs would compete with biofuels and zero-emission propulsion technologies for the same allowances.

If annual demand exceeds the available allowances, allocations would be reduced uniformly across all applicants, regardless of the fuel or technology used, according to the proposal.

Aurelia Leeuw, EU policy director at the SASHA Coalition, echoes those concerns. She thinks the lack of a dedicated RFNBO allocation within the 110 million EUA pool is one of the proposal’s main shortcomings.

She also calls the absence of a long-term offtake requirement a drawback, saying the proposal “doesn’t require long term offtake agreements, which really doesn’t make sense considering that’s an improvement being implemented on the aviation side.”

The EU ETS revision is not yet law. The European Parliament and the Council will negotiate the proposal from this autumn, targeting agreement in the first quarter of 2027 and implementation in 2028.

In other news this week, the Port of Long Beach signed an agreement with the US Maritime Administration to examine how small modular nuclear reactors can be safely accommodated on commercial vessels.

Around 25 mt of CO2 captured during an onboard carbon capture and storage (OCCS) pilot has been officially recognised for compliance under the EU ETS, the Global Centre for Maritime Decarbonisation (GCMD) said. Separately, a GCMD proposal to the IMO for recognising mineralisation of carbon as a permanent CO2 storage secured in-principle support from the global shipping regulator.

Bunker supplier SIPG Energy supplied 2,800 mt of bio-methanol to a dual-fuel car carrier owned by Nordic shipping company Wallenius Wilhelmsen in Shanghai. The bio-methanol stem was delivered to the Arctic Tern by SIPG Energy’s methanol bunker barge Hai Gang Zhi Yuan in a ship-to-ship bunker operation.

Germany’s Hamburg Port Authority (HPA) rolled out safety and operational guidelines for ship-to-ship ammonia bunkering at the port. The guidelines are intended to prepare the Port of Hamburg for future ammonia bunker operations, HPA said.

text:
Every cruise ship you have ever watched pull into a harbor has a funnel, and that funnel is always doing something. Even tied up at the dock with the passengers ashore, a hull that size is burning fuel to run the lights, the galley, the air conditioning and the water treatment plant.

Shore power solves part of it in the handful of ports wired for it. Most ports aren’t.

Viking’s attempt at the rest of that problem is sitting at an outfitting dock on Italy’s Adriatic coast right now. The Viking Libra was floated out at Fincantieri’s Ancona shipyard on March 19, and Viking says it will join the fleet in November.

The specs are modest by cruise standards: 239 meters long, roughly 54,300 gross tons, 499 staterooms, 998 guests. What isn’t modest is the fuel. This is the first cruise ship ever built to store liquefied hydrogen on board and run fuel cells on it.

That much got reported everywhere in March. The number that actually tells you what the ship does showed up two months later, on an earnings call, and almost nobody picked it up.

The fuel cells cover about a third of the propulsion

The hydrogen setup on Libra is a bank of proton exchange membrane fuel cells rated at up to six megawatts, built by Isotta Fraschini Motori, a Fincantieri subsidiary in Bari.

Six megawatts is a shade over 8,000 horsepower of generating capacity, which sounds like a lot right up until you remember it’s shifting a 54,300-ton hotel.

On Viking’s first-quarter call on May 14, an analyst asked chairman Torstein Hagen about the unit economics of the propulsion package. His answer contained a figure that has never appeared in a Viking press release: the fuel cells will cover roughly a third of the ship’s propulsion capacity.

The other two thirds are conventional.

Hagen didn’t dress that up, and he didn’t dress up the fuel either, calling hydrogen expensive and not easy to get hold of. He described the ship as “setting a direction of travel for the future of shipping”, which is a more honest framing than most of the coverage gave it.

Viking’s own written language has been careful about this from the start. The float-out announcement describes a propulsion system “based partially on liquefied hydrogen and fuel cells,” and says the ship will be capable of operating with zero emissions rather than doing it all the time.

Those two words, “partially” and “capable,” are carrying the entire claim.

So the accurate version is this: Libra can shut its engines down and run clean for stretches, in the places where that matters most, and then go back to burning what every other ship burns.

Which is still a first, and still worth building. It is not a hydrogen ship in the way an electric car is an electric car.

The hydrogen arrives in a box, because there is nowhere to plug in

The cleverest thing about this project has nothing to do with the fuel cells.

There is essentially no liquid hydrogen bunkering infrastructure at cruise ports. None. You cannot pull alongside in Bergen or Barcelona and take on LH2 the way you take on diesel, because the pipes and the tanks and the trained crews don’t exist yet.

Fincantieri’s workaround is to skip the dockside infrastructure entirely. Libra takes its hydrogen aboard in containers, loaded during port calls, which the shipbuilder has described as a first-of-its-kind solution to get around exactly that supply chain gap.

It’s the same instinct that produced the shipping container in the first place: if the terminal isn’t built, bring the terminal with you. It also means the ship’s clean-running range is capped by how many containers it can carry and how often it can get them refilled, which is not a small caveat.

We have covered the alternative approach, and it’s worth comparing. The Lithuanian port of Klaipėda went the other way with the harbor tanker Rasa, building the hydrogen plant on the dock and letting the ship stay put.

That works beautifully for a 42-meter boat that never leaves the harbor. It does nothing for a ship whose entire business model is going somewhere else.

Nobody has said where the hydrogen comes from

Fuel cells emit water vapor. That is chemistry and it isn’t in dispute. Where the emissions actually live is upstream, in how the hydrogen was made in the first place.

Most industrial hydrogen today comes from steam methane reforming, which means natural gas in one end and CO2 out the other. Green hydrogen made by electrolysis from renewable power exists, costs considerably more, and is not available in the volumes a cruise fleet would need.

As of the float-out in March, the industrial gas trade press noted that Viking had not confirmed where it will source the hydrogen. I haven’t found a supplier announcement since, and Viking hasn’t published one. Until that lands, the ship’s lifecycle emissions are an open question rather than a settled number.

There’s a second piece of context Viking put on the record itself. Every ship in its ocean fleet carries closed-loop scrubbers, president and CEO Leah Talactac told the same May call, and that hardware is what allows the fleet to run on heavy fuel oil.

Fuel came to about 4% of adjusted gross margin last year. That is the fleet Libra is joining.

Norway’s fjord rule doesn’t touch a ship this size until 2032

The commercial logic usually attached to this ship is the Norwegian fjords, and the timeline there is worth getting right, because a lot of coverage has fudged it.

Norway has adopted zero-emission requirements for the five UNESCO World Heritage fjords: Geirangerfjord, Nærøyfjord, Aurlandsfjord, Sunnylvsfjord and Tafjord. Ships must produce no direct CO2 or methane while inside them, and must connect to shore power where compatible facilities exist.

The catch is the threshold. The Norwegian rules took effect on January 1, 2026 for passenger ships under 10,000 gross tons, and don’t reach ships of 10,000 GT and above until January 1, 2032. At 54,300 GT, Libra is arriving six years before the regulation that would force its hand.

Global rules aren’t much closer either.

The IMO’s Net-Zero Framework, which would put a price on shipping emissions for vessels above 5,000 GT, failed to clear adoption in October 2025 and again at MEPC 84 this spring. The next formal attempt is a one-day resumed session penciled in for December 4, three weeks after Libra is due to be handed over.

So Viking is buying compliance nobody is demanding yet, which is either strategic patience or an expensive hedge depending on how the next few votes go.

Fincantieri’s engine shop just fired a cylinder on pure hydrogen

The fuel cell is only half of what Isotta Fraschini is doing with the molecule, and the other half moved this week.

On July 22 the company reported the first firing of a single-cylinder test engine running on 100% hydrogen, developed with UK consultancy Ricardo under Fincantieri’s EU-backed Wave 2 the Future program. Next step is multi-cylinder testing, which is the stage where you find out whether a research engine can become a product.

That matters because a hydrogen internal combustion engine and a hydrogen fuel cell solve different problems. Fuel cells are efficient and silent and expensive. Combustion engines are cheaper, tolerate scruffier fuel, and slot into an engine room the industry already knows how to build.

There is a third route too: an industrial gas turbine cleared to push a ship on 100% hydrogen, type-approved by RINA at Posidonia in June.

Fincantieri is chasing the first two from the same building in Bari.

Everyone else is moving slower. MSC’s World Europa has carried a fuel cell since 2022, but it’s a 150-kilowatt demonstrator running on LNG rather than hydrogen.

MSC’s Explora V and VI, announced in 2022 with liquid hydrogen containment and a six-megawatt fuel cell for hotel load, are due in 2027 and 2028; Fincantieri’s more recent public description of those two ships refers to fuel cells that convert LNG into hydrogen.

Viking’s own Astrea, also hydrogen, follows in 2027.

The pattern across all of it is the same: the hardware is arriving faster than the fuel.

What to actually watch in November

If you want to judge whether this ship delivers on its billing, ignore the christening photos and watch for two specific things.

The first is a hydrogen supply agreement with a named producer and a named color. Green, blue or grey changes the entire emissions story, and until someone signs, the zero-emission claim only describes what happens at the funnel.

The second is how long Libra can actually run on the cells in service, in hours, on a real itinerary.

A third of propulsion capacity and a container-load of LH2 is a real capability with a real limit, and that limit will show up in the operating schedule long before it shows up in a press release.

text:
Allied Biofuels details export routes for planned $6.1B Uzbekistan SAF project

In New York, The Times of Central Asia reported that Allied Biofuels has disclosed planned export routes that would carry sustainable aviation fuel from its proposed facility in Uzbekistan to customers in Europe and the United Arab Emirates via rail and sea corridors crossing Kazakhstan, the Caspian Sea, the Black Sea, and the Suez Canal.

The routes are set out in a logistics agreement with Latvia-based Pro Logistic Services that was signed during the 5th Tashkent International Investment Forum in June and announced on July 20. It covers the future transport of sustainable aviation fuel and electro-synthetic sustainable aviation fuel (e-SAF), rather than immediate exports. Under the agreement, Pro Logistic Services will design and implement a multimodal transport network covering dedicated rail tank cars, port handling, freight forwarding, and marine shipping. The company would coordinate delivery from the project site in Uzbekistan to customers in Europe, the UAE, and other markets, the report added.

text:
The Yun Tao No. 1 combines fuel cells, batteries, and electric motors to carry heavy loads on the Pearl River, while a fleet of up to 100 ships depends on autonomy, refueling, and competitive cost.

China has launched the Yun Tao No. 1, a hydrogen-powered river cargo ship with a length of 69.3 meters, a capacity of nearly 2,000 tons, and space to transport up to 140 containers. The launch took place on July 16, 2026, in the city of Zhaoqing, in China’s Guangdong province.

The information was published by The Maritime Executive, a publication specialized in maritime transport and navigation. The ship was presented as the largest river cargo ship in China equipped with hydrogen fuel cells and as the first unit of a planned commercial network for the Pearl River region.

The project goes beyond a small vessel created just for demonstration. The proposal places the technology in a commercially sized cargo ship, with a reported autonomy of 760 kilometers and the capacity to carry containers, ore, coal, or grains.

Electrifying a river cargo ship is more difficult than moving a car

A car needs to transport a few people and a limited load. A river cargo ship needs to move hundreds of tons over long distances, maintain constant power, and reserve most of the hull for goods.

Simply increasing the size of the batteries can take up space and add weight. This reduces part of the area that could be used for cargo and requires long recharging periods, depending on the infrastructure available at each terminal.

Hydrogen offers another way to power electric motors. Instead of relying solely on the energy stored in the batteries, the ship generates electricity during the journey through fuel cells.

Even so, the system needs to prove that it works continuously. Autonomy, hydrogen price, safety, and refueling time will have a direct influence on the commercial viability of the vessel.

Yun Tao No. 1 can carry 140 containers and loose cargo

The freighter is 69.3 meters long and has a capacity of nearly 2 thousand tons. On a trip, it can transport up to 140 containers or receive loose cargo, such as ore, coal, and grains.

The vessel was developed by Guangdong Yuntao Hydrogen Energy in partnership with the China State Shipbuilding Corporation, a Chinese state-owned shipbuilding group. The goal is to serve river transport routes in the Pearl River region.

The hull was designed to face less resistance during water displacement. In practice, this means that the shape tries to facilitate the ship’s advancement and reduce the energy needed to maintain navigation.

The project also includes an intelligent alert system for navigation. The feature was designed to help in shallow areas, stretches with strong currents, and zones that require greater environmental care.

Three fuel cells work alongside lithium batteries

The propulsion system uses 3 generator sets of 260 kW, powered by hydrogen. Each set produces electricity, which goes to the equipment responsible for moving the ship.

The fuel cell can be understood as a small plant installed on board. It combines hydrogen and oxygen in a controlled reaction to generate electrical energy, without needing to burn the fuel as in a common engine.

The lithium batteries support this operation. They store part of the energy and can help when the ship needs to respond to speed changes, maneuvers, or variations in engine demand.

The Maritime Executive, a publication specializing in maritime transport and navigation, provided the propulsion system data and the reported autonomy of 760 kilometers. The combination allows distributing energy between the fuel cells and the batteries during operation.

Fleet of 100 ships still depends on refueling and daily operation

Guangdong Yuntao Hydrogen Energy plans to deploy 100 standardized vessels over the next 4 years in the Pearl River region. The quantity represents a business goal and not a fleet already built or in service.

For the plan to progress, the company works with a network that involves hydrogen production, storage, transportation, and refueling. Without stations ready to receive the fuel, the ships may remain idle and lose the advantage of regular operation.

The company also aims to achieve unsubsidized operation by 2028. This outcome still depends on the fuel price, the efficiency of refueling stations, and the actual performance of the vessels.

Operational costs were presented as 20% to 30% lower than those of similar diesel-powered ships. The comparison will still need to be confirmed in commercial routine, as the hydrogen price and infrastructure availability may change the outcome.

Hydrogen on the ship does not mean zero carbon in the whole process

During navigation, the fuel cell does not burn diesel to produce the electricity used by the engines. This can reduce the direct emission of gases and other residues linked to combustion on the ship itself.

However, the environmental impact does not end on the vessel. The origin of the hydrogen defines a large part of the carbon footprint, as the fuel can be produced with different energy sources.

When production uses fossil fuels, part of the emissions occurs before refueling. When the electricity used in manufacturing comes from low-emission sources, the environmental result can be more favorable.

This also includes the storage, transportation of hydrogen, and the energy consumed to deliver the fuel to the ship. Therefore, the analysis needs to consider the entire path, from production to use.

Technology could be tested in Brazilian river corridors

In a simple comparison, Yun Tao No. 1 combines the cargo and propulsion system in the same hull. In corridors that use barges, a vessel can push several loaded compartments, forming a larger set.

A similar application in Brazil would require its own studies. Each river presents different conditions of depth, distance, current, transported volume, and access to terminals.

The biggest obstacle would be creating a secure supply network. It wouldn’t be enough to buy the ship. It would be necessary to produce or transport the hydrogen, keep the fuel stored near the route, and refuel the vessel without interrupting the operation for long periods.

The Chinese project can help show how fuel cells and batteries behave in heavy transport. However, the commercial performance of the first ship will be more important than the launch to indicate whether the technology can scale up.

The entry of Yun Tao No. 1 into the water marks the attempt to bring hydrogen to a river cargo ship with commercial capacity. Its 69.3 meters, the 140 containers, and the reported range of 760 kilometers place the project above small demonstration tests.

The potential fleet of 100 ships still depends on concrete results in safety, cost, and refueling. The first cargo ship will have to show if it can work every day without losing payload, range, or time at the terminals.

title: Why Maritime Decarbonisation is the Caribbean's Next Climate Battleground
description:
The global maritime sector is undergoing an environmental overhaul that is driven by an urgent mandate to eliminate its carbon footprint.
The global framework for this transformation was solidified when the International Maritime Organization (IMO) adopted its historic 2023 GHG Strategy.
This milestone agreement set highly ambitious targets, aiming to slash greenhouse gas emissions and reach a net-zero trajectory for international shipping by or around 2050.
Historically, the Caribbean faced a severe capacity deficit at this specialized intersection of climate science, maritime law, and economic policy.
By focusing on technical advisory work, delegate training, and regional coordination, UWI-CSL has quickly built up the Caribbean’s diplomatic muscle, especially at the IMO.
text:
The global maritime sector is undergoing an environmental overhaul that is driven by an urgent

mandate to eliminate its carbon footprint. For the Caribbean, this is an existential reality and not

merely an abstract policy discussion happening on distant shores. As Small Island Developing

States, the Caribbean’s relationship with the sea is two-fold as it is on the front lines of climate

change, yet completely reliant on marine transport to sustain daily life.

Maritime shipping serves as the heartbeat of Caribbean economies, delivering between 80%

and 90% of all imported food consumed in the region, while sharing its waters with a tourism

sector that commands roughly 43% of global cruise traffic. Decarbonizing this sector therefore,

is a high-stakes balancing act. If done poorly, new international regulations could drive up

freight costs and severely threaten regional food security. If executed equitably, however, it

offers a generational opportunity for the Caribbean to transition away from imported fossil fuels

and catalyze a resilient green economy.

The global framework for this transformation was solidified when the International Maritime

Organization (IMO) adopted its historic 2023 GHG Strategy. This milestone agreement set

highly ambitious targets, aiming to slash greenhouse gas emissions and reach a net-zero

trajectory for international shipping by or around 2050. However, the true test of this strategy

lies in the ongoing negotiation and adoption of subsequent short and mid-term measures.

These technical regulations and economic mechanisms, such as global fuel standards and

maritime carbon pricing systems, will dictate the immediate financial realities of global trade. For

vulnerable island economies like ours, participating in the design of these near-term measures

is vital. Without a strong and unified regional voice, these impending emission penalties could

unfairly penalize the region’s import-dependent nations before they have the infrastructure to

adapt.

Historically, the Caribbean faced a severe capacity deficit at this specialized intersection of

climate science, maritime law, and economic policy. This gap became increasingly visible during

the Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC) 80 negotiations where key

decarbonization frameworks were finalized, and seeing only four out of sixteen Caribbean IMO

member states represented.

To reverse this trend and secure a fair transition, regional stakeholders mobilized, culminating in

the August 2024 launch of the University of the West Indies Caribbean Shipping Lanes Project

(UWI-CSL). Housed at the Shridath Ramphal Centre (SRC), UWI-CSL was designed to address

these deficiencies.

By focusing on technical advisory work, delegate training, and regional coordination, UWI-CSL

has quickly built up the Caribbean’s diplomatic muscle, especially at the IMO. The project has

already facilitated national consultations across several countries and successfully delivered the

first-ever joint Caribbean submission to the IMO. Through the evidence-based support of UWI-

CSL, regional leaders are no longer passive bystanders , as they are now actively shaping

global maritime policy to ensure the green transition is both impactful and equitable for the

Caribbean.

Submitted by the UWI-Caribbean Shipping Lanes Project (UWI-CSL)

When obtained through sustainable processes, Wärtsilä estimates it can reduce total greenhouse gas emissions by at least 90% compared to equivalent diesel engines.
Moreover, the Wärtsilä 25 Ammonia engine is part of the company’s strategy to expand the use of alternative fuels in the maritime sector.

text:
Wärtsilä will supply Wärtsilä 25 Ammonia auxiliary engines and propulsion systems for two vessels intended to transport LPG and liquid ammonia.

Finnish technology group Wärtsilä will supply its Wärtsilä 25 Ammonia auxiliary engine for two new mid-size gas carriers. The vessels will have a capacity of 51,350 cubic meters and will be prepared to transport liquefied petroleum gas and liquid ammonia.

In addition to the ammonia engine, the package will include a selective catalytic reduction system to control nitrogen oxide emissions and a gas valve unit. The company will also deliver a propulsion system with a controllable-pitch propeller.

Two vessels built in Shanghai

The vessels will be built at Nantong CIMC Sinopacific Offshore & Engineering facilities in Shanghai. They will be owned by Navigator Amon Shipping AS, a joint venture created by Navigator Gas and Norway’s Amon Maritime.

Likewise, Wärtsilä will integrate the shaft line and the propulsion solution with the aim of improving operational efficiency. The controllable-pitch propeller system will make it possible to adapt thrust to sailing conditions and reduce energy consumption.

The company booked the order for the engines, the SCR system and the gas valve unit during the second quarter of 2026. The contract related to the propeller system was booked in the third quarter of the same year. Deliveries of the equipment are scheduled to begin in June 2027.

Ammonia gains ground as a marine fuel

The project is being developed as shipping looks for alternatives to conventional diesel; ammonia can be used as a fuel without releasing carbon dioxide during combustion, although its overall climate impact depends on the method used to produce it.

When obtained through sustainable processes, Wärtsilä estimates it can reduce total greenhouse gas emissions by at least 90% compared to equivalent diesel engines.

Moreover, the Wärtsilä 25 Ammonia engine is part of the company’s strategy to expand the use of alternative fuels in the maritime sector. In 2023, Wärtsilä introduced a commercial four-stroke solution designed to run on ammonia.

Lower emissions and greater operational flexibility

The combination of the ammonia engine, the SCR system and controllable-pitch propulsion aims to reduce atmospheric emissions without limiting the vessels’ operational capability.

According to Navigator Gas, selecting the Wärtsilä 25 Ammonia will reduce the vessels’ environmental impact and facilitate their adaptation to increasingly stringent maritime regulations.

In addition, the SCR system will reduce NOx emissions generated during combustion; this component will be relevant for operating in areas with stricter environmental controls.

A project linked to maritime decarbonization

The International Maritime Organization continues to use net-zero emissions in shipping by 2050 as a benchmark. In that scenario, fuels such as ammonia, methanol and synthetic fuels are taking an increasingly prominent place in shipowners’ and manufacturers’ plans.

However, the expansion of ammonia as a marine fuel will depend on factors such as its availability, its cost and the development of port infrastructure. It will also require specific safety systems due to its toxicity.

With these two vessels, Navigator Amon Shipping will add a platform designed to operate with lower emissions and adapt to future regulatory conditions. For Wärtsilä, the contract strengthens its presence in the market for ammonia marine engines and integrated propulsion solutions.
